entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: In John von Neumann's death on February 8, 1957, the world of mathematics lost a most original, penetrating, and versatile mind. Science suffered the loss of a universal intellect and a unique interpreter of mathematics, who could bring the latest (and develop latent) applications of its methods to bear on problems of physics, astronomy, biology, and the new technology.
entries.work: S. Ulam, “John von Neumann, 1903–1957,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 64 (3), Part 2 (May 1958), pp. 1–49
entries.context: The article's first sentences. The paragraph continues: “Many eminent voices have already described and praised his contributions. It is my aim to add here a brief account of his life and of his work from a background of personal acquaintance and friendship extending over a period of 25 years.”
entries.caution: Read from the author's on-disk OCR transcription of the BAMS memorial at 02_VON_NEUMANN/Ulam_von_Neumann_Obituary_BAMS_1958.md, not from the printed issue or the Project Euclid scan. That transcription splits words across the original line breaks (e.g. ‘organ izational’, ‘con tains’); this passage contains no such split. Page number derived from the running-head markers in the same file.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: Johnny was regarded by many as an excellent chairman of committees (this peculiar contemporary activity). He would press strongly his technical views, but defer rather easily on personal or organizational matters.
entries.work: S. Ulam, “John von Neumann, 1903–1957,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 64 (3), Part 2 (May 1958), pp. 1–49
entries.context: Stands as its own paragraph, between Ulam's account of von Neumann's conversational evaluations of other scientists and his account of von Neumann's lack of a certain self-confidence.
entries.caution: Read from the author's on-disk OCR transcription at 02_VON_NEUMANN/Ulam_von_Neumann_Obituary_BAMS_1958.md. The OCR renders this paragraph without word-splitting. Page number derived from the running-head markers in the same file.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: In October, 1954, he was named by presidential appointment as a member of the United States Atomic Energy Commission. He left Princeton on a leave of absence and discontinued all commitments with the exception of the chairmanship of the ICBM Committee. Admiral Strauss, chairman of the Commission and a friend of Johnny's for many years, suggested this nomination as soon as a vacancy occurred.
entries.work: S. Ulam, “John von Neumann, 1903–1957,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 64 (3), Part 2 (May 1958), pp. 1–49
entries.context: Immediately followed in the printing by an indented quotation from Lewis Strauss beginning “During the period between the date of his confirmation and the late autumn, 1955, Johnny functioned magnificently…”
entries.caution: Read from the author's on-disk OCR transcription at 02_VON_NEUMANN/Ulam_von_Neumann_Obituary_BAMS_1958.md. In that transcription the word ‘occurred’ is broken by a page turn as ‘oc curred’; it is restored here to its printed form without brackets because the split is an OCR artefact of the line break, not a feature of the printing. Page number derived from the running-head markers in the same file.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: An incomplete list of scientific and organizational activities contains the following positions: From 1940-1957, he was a member of the Scientific Advisory Committee, Ballistic Research Laboratories, Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland; the Navy Bureau of Ordnance, Washington, D. C. from 1941-1955; consultant to Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory 1943-1955; also the Naval Ordnance Laboratory, Silver Spring, Maryland from 1947-1955; member of the Research and Development Board, Washington, D. C. 1949-1953; a consultant to the Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Tennessee 1949-1954; member from 1950 to 1955 of the Armed Forces Special Weapons Project, Washington, D. C; also in Washington a member of the Scientific Advisory Board, U. S. Air Force, Washington, D. C. 1951-1957; a member of the General Advisory Committee by presidential appointment 1952-1954; and on the Technical Advisory Panel on Atomic Energy, Washington, D. C. 1953-1957; Chairman of the Advisory Committee on Guided Missiles (1954-1957 with Clark Millikan as acting chairman in 1956).
entries.work: S. Ulam, “John von Neumann, 1903–1957,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 64 (3), Part 2 (May 1958), pp. 1–49
entries.context: The list Ulam promises earlier in the memorial when he writes that “A list of his positions, organizational memberships, etc., will be found at the end of this article.” It appears in the closing biographical apparatus before the bibliography of von Neumann's publications.
entries.caution: Read from the author's on-disk OCR transcription at 02_VON_NEUMANN/Ulam_von_Neumann_Obituary_BAMS_1958.md. That transcription splits five words across original line breaks — ‘con tains’, ‘Scien tific’, ‘presi dential’ — and renders one date range as ‘1949- 1954’ with an inserted space; all four are rejoined here as printed, without brackets, because the splits are OCR artefacts of line breaks. The comma-for-period after ‘Washington, D. C’ is as the OCR gives it and has not been corrected. Page number derived from the running-head markers in the same file.

entries.speaker: Claude Shannon
entries.quote: Involving a mixture of pure and applied mathematics as well as other sciences, automata theory was an ideal field for von Neumann's wide-ranging intellect. He brought to it many new insights and opened up at least two new directions of research. It is unfortunate that he was unable to complete the work he had in progress, some of which is in the form of rough notes or unedited lectures, and for some of which no record exists apart from his colleagues' memories of casual conversations.
entries.work: Claude E. Shannon, “Von Neumann's Contributions to Automata Theory,” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 64 (3), Part 2 (May 1958), pp. 123–129
entries.context: Shannon's article is the companion piece to Ulam's memorial in the same BAMS memorial issue. Shannon's bibliography item [12] is described there as “Unfinished manuscript for the University of Illinois Press relating to the theory of automata and, particularly, self-reproducing machines.”
entries.caution: Retrieved by web fetch of the AMS-hosted scan of the printed article, which passes page content through an intermediate summarising model; not read from a printed copy or a raw PDF by this agent. Page number as reported by that fetch.

entries.speaker: Nicholas Metropolis
entries.quote: I went twice to Chicago, once in '46 and then another time in late '57. I arrived in Chicago when Sputnik was——October 4, 1957 is the date of Sputnik. I arrived in Chicago on that date and I went there and stayed there for about eight years.
entries.work: Nicholas Metropolis, oral history interview conducted by Richard Rhodes; transcript published by the Atomic Heritage Foundation / National Museum of Nuclear Science & History, Voices of the Manhattan Project
entries.context: Metropolis is distinguishing his two periods at the University of Chicago. The second, beginning 4 October 1957, is the period in which he was professor of physics and founding director of the university's Institute for Computer Research.
entries.caution: A transcriber's rendering of spoken words, not a text written by Metropolis. Published by the Atomic Heritage Foundation with their transcription conventions; the double em-dash marking a self-interruption is as the transcript gives it. Retrieved by web fetch, which passes page content through an intermediate summarising model; the transcript page is unpaginated.

entries.speaker: Nicholas Metropolis
entries.quote: I was in charge of the research on computers and designed a computer. We thought we would try to develop computer engineering as opposed to electronic engineering, thereby training people who were electronic engineers to learn about computer engineering.
entries.work: Nicholas Metropolis, oral history interview conducted by Richard Rhodes; transcript published by the Atomic Heritage Foundation / National Museum of Nuclear Science & History, Voices of the Manhattan Project
entries.context: Metropolis is describing his own role at Los Alamos. In the surrounding transcript he goes on to mention a year spent at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton before returning to organise the Los Alamos work.
entries.caution: A transcriber's rendering of spoken words. Retrieved by web fetch through an intermediate summarising model; transcript unpaginated. Metropolis does not in this passage name a division, group number or job title.

entries.speaker: Herbert L. Anderson
entries.quote: After the war Nick joined the faculty of the University of Chicago, to help set up a major computing facility. When that didn't materialize as quickly as he had hoped, he began to think of other possibilities, and about that time he got a call from Carson Mark, head of the Theoretical Division at Los Alamos, suggesting that he set up a computing facility here. Nick was ready, willing, and able. The moral of my story is that fortune favors the prepared mind. Nick was right there, well prepared to do just what he was asked to do, and that's how the MANIAC was born.
entries.work: Herbert L. Anderson, “Metropolis, Monte Carlo, and the MANIAC,” Los Alamos Science No. 14 (1986), pp. 96–108
entries.context: Anderson is recounting Metropolis's 1948 return to Los Alamos. ‘Here’ is Los Alamos; ‘Nick’ is Metropolis throughout the article.
entries.caution: Anderson is a colleague writing about Metropolis; these are Anderson's words, not Metropolis's. Retrieved by web fetch of the LANL-hosted scan, which passes page content through an intermediate summarising model; not read from a printed copy by this agent. Page number as reported by that fetch.

entries.speaker: Herbert L. Anderson
entries.quote: MANIAC II succeeded MANIAC I in Los Alamos in 1956. The second MANIAC was more powerful than the first and, because it included floating-point arithmetic, was easier to use. MANIAC III, with the latest in solid-state circuitry, was developed at the University of Chicago when Nick returned there to head the newly formed Institute for Computer Research.
entries.work: Herbert L. Anderson, “Metropolis, Monte Carlo, and the MANIAC,” Los Alamos Science No. 14 (1986), pp. 96–108
entries.context: Anderson's summary of the MANIAC line. He gives no year for the Chicago move and no year for MANIAC III.
entries.caution: Anderson's words, not Metropolis's. Anderson dates MANIAC II to 1956; the English Wikipedia article on Metropolis dates it to 1957 and the Atomic Heritage Foundation profile says Metropolis ‘oversaw the construction of MANIAC II’ in 1957 with MANIAC I shut down in 1958 — the printings disagree and this record reproduces Anderson's. Retrieved by web fetch of the LANL-hosted scan through an intermediate summarising model. Page number as reported by that fetch.

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: Despite the comfort of the Los Alamos Lab (in the fifties and sixties Ulam was one of two research advisors to the Director of the lab), Stan could not find peace there. He became a permanent traveler. Ever since he returned to Los Alamos in 1946 he had lived, unbelievable as it may sound, out of a suitcase.
entries.context: Rota is describing Ulam's life at Los Alamos in the decade after the hydrogen bomb. The preceding sentences describe Ulam's new standing as “an international celebrity and as the resident genius of the Los Alamos Laboratory” and record that “His attention span, already short, now decreased to a dangerous low.”
entries.caution: Rota's characterisation of Ulam, not Ulam's own words. Read from the author's on-disk transcription of Indiscrete Thoughts at 04_ROTA/Indiscrete Thoughts.md; the bracketed page markers in that file ([78]) are the transcription's own and locate this passage on p. 78. Rota does not name the second research adviser.

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: The traits of Stan Ulam's personality that became dominant in his later years were laziness, generosity, considerateness, and most of all, incisiveness of thought.
entries.context: Followed in the printing by: “Those who knew Stan and did not know what to make of him covered up the mixture of envy and resentment they felt toward him by pronouncing him lazy. He was proverbially lazy.”
entries.caution: Rota's characterisation of Ulam, not Ulam's own words. Read from the author's on-disk transcription at 04_ROTA/Indiscrete Thoughts.md; the transcription's bracketed page marker [80] falls immediately after the sentences that follow this one.

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: His generosity was curiously linked to his laziness. A generous action is often impulsive, and calls for little foresight. Its opposite requires the careful advance planning that Stan loathed.
entries.context: Immediately following Rota's account of Ulam asking him “Isn't it true that I am a charlatan?” and preceding “He fancied himself a grand seigneur of bottomless means…”
entries.caution: Rota's characterisation of Ulam, not Ulam's own words. Read from the author's on-disk transcription at 04_ROTA/Indiscrete Thoughts.md; the transcription's bracketed page marker [81] falls in the sentence immediately preceding.

entries.speaker: Stanislaw Ulam
entries.quote: Of course he worked, in answer to your question. In fact he was unable to play the role of senior scientist or advisor without being actively engaged, like with computing. Even towards the end of his life, when he was chairman of the Intercontinental Ballistic Missile (ICBM) Committee, a committee established by the President after Sputnik.
entries.work: “Ulam and Rota discuss von Neumann,” conversation at Gainesville, Florida; published by MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews
entries.context: Ulam is answering Rota's question “But actual work?” about von Neumann at Los Alamos.
entries.caution: A transcribed conversation; the MacTutor editors state “We have made a few small editorial changes to the text.” Read from the author's on-disk conversion of the MacTutor page (captured 2026-03-01), which is not reproduced in this collection. Ulam's dating is internally inconsistent with the printed record: von Neumann died 8 February 1957 and Sputnik launched 4 October 1957, so the ICBM committee he chaired cannot have been established after Sputnik; Ulam's own 1958 BAMS memorial dates the chairmanship of the Advisory Committee on Guided Missiles to 1954–1957. The text this was read from is not reproduced in this collection; the work is cited to its published edition in URLS.md.

entries.speaker: Freeman Dyson
entries.quote: When von Neumann tragically died, the snobs took their revenge and got rid of the computing project root and branch
entries.work: Quoted by Jim Holt, “How the Computers Exploded,” The New York Review of Books, 7 June 2012 (review of George Dyson, Turing's Cathedral)
entries.date: date of utterance not established; quoted 2012
entries.context: Holt's sentence reads in full: “‘When von Neumann tragically died, the snobs took their revenge and got rid of the computing project root and branch,’ the author's father, Freeman Dyson, later commented, adding that ‘the demise of our computer group was a disaster not only for Princeton but for science as a whole.’”
